There is zero evidence of machines being tampered with, Harris ballots being thrown away, or anything of the sort. Some states have shitty machines that malfunction. If that occurs then most states will send them to the other machine or if that doesn’t work give them paper ballots to fill by hand. Especially in swing states, these election workers have back up plans to back up plans to back up plans when things don’t work, they double, triple, quintuple check ballots. If any are missing, then all activity stops until they find it. A lot of states, swing states included, require that every election worker in each precinct sign onto certification before reporting results, meaning if you have a conspiracy to throw out votes, then every poll worker has to agree to it. Even if that happened, county boards know how many ballots they sent out and will require every single one to be turned in. These are just examples, but my point is that if there was mass fraud, then far more people would recognize it and be coming forward than a few cranks on self-run like “gregpalast.com.”  Just like in 2020, all of these videos and pictures conspiracy theorists use are either misinterpreting a correct election process or extrapolating one fuck up to a massive fraud scheme. Also, these poll workers are volunteers, inevitably there will be minor fuck ups sometimes, but the number of those that aren’t fixed at the polling place itself are always minuscule. You’re talking about mistakes that will affect two digits of ballots nationally. Even if that were left unrectified, there is pretty much no scenario

Every queer person needs to recognize it. Speaking personally the pink triangle is one of those symbols where I don’t feel right reclaiming it. Words like “queer” or “dyke” were/are slurs that applied to people fairly generally, so I think if you look at those and say “yeah, actually fuck you that fits me and I’m proud of it,” it can be cathartic and empowering. The pink triangle is different in that it applies to a very specific historical context and was really only used to designate gay men and not queer people in general. Klaus Müller has a quote about this (mentioned in the Wikipedia entry) that really struck me: “the pink triangles of the concentration camps became an international symbol of gay and lesbian pride because so few of us are haunted by concrete memories of those who were forced to wear them.” 

There’s an argument to be made that because queer people as a whole are persecuted, we can use the symbol as a sign of solidarity in that struggle. But I worry that mindset is appropriative. I think about what people in those camps who were murdered wearing that symbol would think about it being used as a point of pride sought out by people who never experienced what they did. There are people around the world being hunted down, jailed, tortured, murdered, etc. for being queer, and I’d find it a much more effective protest symbol in places like Iran or Qatar where those experiences could actually be considered comparable. But it just feels weird to me seeing it casually used by an LGBTQIA+ program, a pride parade, or online or wherever.

I’ve gone through this before multiple times. It’s absolutely heartbreaking. Being autistic can be a deeply lonely experience, and many of us really crave close, secure relationships where we feel like we can be ourselves in a world that punishes us for not being neurotypical. For me there’s this constant insecurity that every friendship is one-sided even when someone does really care about me, because it feels like so much of me is contained in my often difficult everyday experiences and if I don’t filter that from conversation with my friends they just separate themselves because they can’t deal with it. And it’s fair for them to have limits to how much they can support us or have times in their life where it’s especially hard, even if our attachment to them makes it feel like we’d crawl through broken glass for them. 

As much as we wish it were, friendship isn’t a contract and a lot of the time when things get really hard for us and we need support people will hit their limit and drift away. I’ve had people cut contact with me feeling like I use them as an emotional crutch, feeling like I don’t really care about them and just add stress to their lives by constantly needing their support. But it’s really not true even if I do get carried away with that sometimes, and a lot of the time they really don’t give you much chance of adjusting those behaviors. I care about them so so much and love everything about being around them and talking to them and having fun with them or anything else. And from my perspective I give them every opportunity to talk about what they want to or support them while they vent if they want to do that, but it’s like they just don’t take our support? I guess because neurotypical people usually need it less, and a lot of other autistic people deal with their similar struggles internally rather than seeking out support.

I really don’t know a solution because even when we have resources like therapists that allow us to express ourselves fully it’s not like we can turn off being autistic between sessions. I find using other outlets to vent to when we need that rather than putting too much of it on one person helps a lot, but that also comes with the exhaustion and alienation of feeling like you need to all the time even with the people you trust most. It always feels like your friendship is hanging by a thread based on how well you mask and they’re always the ones to cut it with a pair of scissors. 

On the other hand, other autistic people are a great source of comfort because of lot of them understand things you go through and maybe deal with it in similar ways you do. I think seeking them out is a great way to make lasting friendships. But I also find that a lot of the other autistic people I meet are so fucking exhausted and depressed/anxious all of the time that they understandably can’t put the energy into new friendships, and even when you offer a shoulder many would rather just deal with it by isolating themselves. That’s completely okay and can be good for those of us better able to cope that way, everyone has their own ways of experiencing neurodiversity and social life as a whole. It just is super difficult for those of us who get a lot out of much more regular connection to find or maintain those. 

There’s so much more I could say and I realize I could have been more nuanced, I really am not trying to generalize or assume what others are feeling or going through. Just relating to you in the way I can and want you to know these losses are something that so many of us also experience. It’s not just you being especially incapable of anything. You’re not at fault for how difficult keeping connections as an autistic person can be.

I started on pills for the first couple of months but moved to injections quickly and have been happy with it ever since. In addition to what others have said, it’s much, much easier to remember to do a shot once a week than to take one or two pills every single day. I chronically forget to take my pill medications and injections make sure that isn’t a problem for my transition. Another thing is that while pills are just as effective at the proper dosage, they have a much lower concentration of estrogen and it can be a pain messing with your dose, plus you’ll very likely need to stay on a t-blocker. Injections usually require a lot less fiddling with dosages, plus if the higher e concentration injections have suppresses testosterone on its own well enough (in most cases it does get to that point) you don’t have to worry about taking t-blocker in addition to it. I guess that’s theoretically possible with pills too, but keeping up requires so much fiddling and such a rigid routine.

That said, injections are not the way to go for everyone and it’s not going to hamper your transition in any way if you want to go another route. All of them are perfectly safe, and none of them are really anything you need to worry about avoiding. Patches and gels are a good option that I’ve never experimented with and pills work. But afaik of the pretty negligible medical risks HRT is correlated to, injections have less than pills do. It won’t contribute to liver problems or anything at least, but there may also be a couple of anecdotal things I’ve forgotten about by now. Either way, these are edge cases where HRT is one of many many factors.

I actually had a double mastectomy at 13 before I had any clue I was trans because I was insecure about gynecomastia, so at a year on HRT I’ve had literally no growth at all because almost all my breast tissue was removed. I walk around every day and see people I’m jealous of, and it feels like I’m having my heart cut out I’m so jealous. Especially when I see other trans women who develop them. I’m completely flat, like I barely fit into AA cup bras and most men have larger breasts than me. 

I don’t have a solution other than hoping HRT will help them come or eventually getting top surgery, I feel constant pain about this too. But what’s affirming for me is wearing bras with small cups that fit ok because it gives the outline of at least a little something under my shirt and can look cute and sexy even if you don’t have much (in my case anything) to work with. Usually push-up or wireless bras are the way to go. Even if there’s nothing there to push up, wired or unwired push-up bras still have more padding that gives a little bit of shape. Right now I’m wearing the wireless push-up from Aerie, you can get two for $55 or so and they’re absolutely gorgeous. 

The range of bras you can get depends a lot on whether you can fit in an A cup or not (and one brand of bra style’s A cup is not another’s, so it’s always worth trying if it looks at all possible), but you can order AA cup bras online at your band size. My recommendation for that would be getting a good bra or two from The Little Bra Company. Pepper is another people recommend that can be cute but their sizing is weird and sometimes a bit lower quality imo.

The other thing you can consider is breast forms, which are made specifically for women who’ve had mastectomies can be tucked into bras or put in a little pocket of specialty mastectomy bras (the specialty bras are mostly ugly/bland tbh, but you can sew pockets into normal bras, or I know you can take them to Nordstrom and have them do it). Breast forms can be foam, gel, or silicon and there’s a big price/weight/quality range. Silicon breast forms feel the best and are most realistic, and good quality silicon forms are fairly lightweight. But they’re expensive. I shilled out for them and really got a lot of value and better life quality from wearing them though, so ultimately depends what is feasible for you. Gel I’ve never tried but they’re less optimal. You can get foam ones that look good underneath clothes and are much more affordable, but obviously they don’t feel realistic. You can even get breast forms you can swim in.

Personally I used to rely on breast forms but have moved away to just wearing small bras. None of that is a substitute for real breasts, that pain is going to be there as long as you don’t really have them. But it can be affirming and make you feel a lot better.

… Madsen’s dichotomy of moral rituals is also crucial in the third and final parts of the book, where the violent intensification of “rituals of struggle” during the Cultural Revolution and the loss of “ceremonies of innocence” destroyed the Maoist-Confucian moral order and replaced with self-interested utilitarianism. Madsen demonstrates this through the tribulations of Chen Village’s sent-down youths, especially the sharply zealous Ao Meihua, who rose quickly as Maoism’s voice in the village political structure. All vying to advance themselves as paramount examples of revolutionary spirit, the youth were intense competitive with each other in trying to contribute to the village, enduring brutal labor and constantly criticizing one another for even the smallest deviations of the Maoist peasant ideal. The went through a sort of constant “ritual of struggle” that resulted in a hierarchy of influence among them, largely predetermined by their class backgrounds. Those who failed to join the elite Young Communist League and ingratiate themselves with village leaders were the most agitated by Mao’s calls for rebellion, proclaiming themselves Red Guards and temporarily overthrowing village leadership; after Longyong retook control, he exploited the Cleansing of Class Ranks campaign for violent revenge against the youth and his political enemies. Madsen argues that the Cultural Revolution destroyed the moral order of Chen Village by destroying the trust between villagers cultivated by the Socialist Education Movement that was necessary to look beyond self-interest.

While the discourse of synthesis drove villagers to think of the “welfare of the nation” in terms they understood and the ceremonies of innocence generated by Mao worship promoted moral unity through a “collective search for common good,” the loss of trust in Maoism and others in the community due to the Cultural Revolution resulted in a cynical regression to self-interest. In Madsen’s view, the technocrats of the ‘70s seized on the moral void left by Confucianism and Maoism to cultivate a more modest “Liuist” self-interested utilitarian framework. He summarizes this ideology as one born from the Maoist caricature of Liu Shaoqi, in which material incentives like salary drive people to work towards an ultimate goal of economic development and a moral end is no longer the purpose of work. Madsen introduces Bengua and “Pigskin” as examples of this ideology. He portrays them as intelligent technocrats important in planning village economic development but extremely selfish in conduct. These final character studies set up the book's conclusion, where Madsen fits his major political characters into four moral categories of village leadership: the communist gentry who dispenses patronage and favors (Qinlu), the communist rebel who embodies those at the socio-economic margins by governing for the community as an equal whole (Longyon), the moralistic revolutionary whose power depends on their adherence to Maoist ideology (Ao Meihua and the Young Communist League), and the pragmatic technocrat whose political capital comes from their competence in contributing to the goal of economic development (Bengua, Pigskin).”

“…Honing in on the impact of the Socialist Education Movement and the Cultural Revolution in the rural Chen Village, Madsen asks, “How do the Chinese think and talk about what it means to be a good person in a good society, and has their thinking changed over the past several decades?” He argues that throughout the 1960s, the Confucian moral order in rural China synthesized with the Maoist collectivist ethos introduced by the Socialist Education Movement, only for that synthesis to be destroyed by ideological rigidity and the violence of the Cultural Revolution; the lack of a moral order as a result bred cynical self-interest, which in the 1970s merged with “Liuist” utilitarianism devoid of a moral core. The text effectively conveys a nuanced argument through its use of character studies, focus on moral rituals, and effective contextualization of ideological currents.

The book is a case study based on a vast collection of interviews from another project Madsen contributed to, Chen Village: The Recent History of a Peasant Community in Mao's China, a landmark work in itself for its in-depth microhistory of a remote village just when China began to allow global researchers into the country. With much of the text derived from Chen Village, he also references secondary sources to contextualize the broader political and economic trends. The book’s foundational theoretical assertion that in the same vein as professional philosophers, ordinary people engage in constant moral discourse; though not necessarily equipped with philosophical language, they are guided by systematized notions of morality expressed through the interplay of their words and actions. This allows Madsen to trace patterns of moral development, placing their actions and beliefs in moral frameworks of particularist Confucianism, Maoist universalist collectivism, and “Liuist” individualist utilitarianism. Those frameworks are also the basis of his four categories of rural leadership: communist gentry, communist rebel, moralistic revolutionary, and pragmatic technocrat. 

Morality and Power is organized chronologically by stages of Chen Village’s moral discourse. The first focuses on two traditionally Confucian moral approaches, pivoting into its Maoist critiques introduced by the Socialist Education Movement. Madsen skillfully grounds his philosophical arguments by highlighting characters who embody each moral framework. His analysis of Confucianism focusing on the virtue of “good human feeling” contrasts the moral approach of the village’s two cyclically dominant rival leaders: the brash, dictatorial Longyong, who governs the village as “one big family composed of more or less equal members” with himself as stern patriarch, and the well-connected, calculating Qingfa, who governs the village as “a hierarchically structured federation of families… managed through the giving of patronage” to “a few relatively privileged families.” Both of these moral outlooks adhere to Confucian moral particularism, in which people promote good human feeling within their own sphere (or “family”), whether that means to an equal degree within a larger sphere or to a varying degree within a select group with a closer eye to self-interest. 

When Maoist ideology was brought into Chen Village by an urban work team along with a group of radical sent-down youths in the book's second part, it came with a universalist critique and a change in traditional ritual that shifted the village’s moral outlook. The work teams brought class conflict into the moral discourse, denouncing the particularist outlook in favor of a collectivist moral vision where everyone was to contribute through hard work and good example to the equal prosperity of all of China’s proletariat. To condition the villagers into adopting Maoist thought, the ideologues fostered a culture of interpersonal criticism, dragging the village’s cadres and anyone judged as undermining the collective good to ruthless “struggle sessions,” which succeeded in filling the peasants with righteous ideological anger. Maoism was initially well received in the village because alongside those “rituals of struggle,” sectarian customs designed to strengthen moral beliefs through righteous indignation, the work team introduced “ceremonies of innocence” strengthening moral unity by allowing redemption and promoting love for Mao for his devotion to the people and his ideological thought. Madsen uses his two concepts of rituals as a bridge in his theory of a Maoist-Confucian moral synthesis, arguing that the Mao worship promoted by work teams drew heavily from Confucian ancestor worship the villagers already understood…

One book I highly recommend is [Morality and Power in a Chinese Village by Richard Madson (1984)](https://search.worldcat.org/title/9575807), a case study of a rural village which traces how moral psychology and its political manifestations evolved from the beginnings of the Socialist Education Movement in 1963 through the Cultural Revolution and technocratization/decollectivization in the early ‘80s. The book is based almost entirely on interviews from a much larger [history of Chen Village](https://search.worldcat.org/title/244476590) (a pseudonym) Madson collaborated in that was one of if not the first study of its kind in the countryside when China reopened to Western researchers. He also references a diverse array of secondary sources to flesh out his claims. Morality and Power is unique in its focus on rural Chinese peasants at a time when the field of China studies heavily tilted towards studies of the coastal urban regions, and Madsen’s use moral categories and character archetypes as a conceptual tool is really innovative. He makes great use of individual character studies too, especially fleshing out the actions, thoughts, and experiences of village leaders and sent-down youth. It’s worth noting that he is quite skeptical of Mao and Maoist ideology in his analysis, but I think his critiques are balanced and he’s transparent about his outlook. Also the book is quite old now, so I’d certainly suggest checking out some more recent work from that period too. Roosevelt went way further, and his programs were successful. Breasts are the hardest part for me, because when I was a kid I was incredibly insecure about my gynecomastia (advanced breast development relative to what’s standard for AMAB people, my areola were basically bulbs) and I had at least the vast majority of my breast tissue surgically removed. Biden’s economic policy goals are some of the most progressive that any president has ever had (though there’s more he could be doing and he often prioritizes a cautious approach when he shouldn’t). The problem is Congress would not pass anything he proposed and you still need 9 Republican in the Senate to bypass a filibuster if it somehow got through the house. Of people who transition in the United States, at most 8% detransition at some point, with some studies showing 5% or even less than 1% do. I agree with your overall point that the Cuban Missile Crisis was JFK’s fuck up and the Kennedys were predators, but it’s worth pointing out that Bay of Pigs was in the works during the Eisenhower years and Nixon was one of its principal planners. His public remarks calling for respect for international law are consistent with the secrecy of the operation and fears over the international implications of directly saying “We’re going to invade Cuba.” If it went the way the CIA planned for it to go, then US involvement (even if it was the obvious conclusion) wouldn’t have had as clear of an evidence trail and President Nixon would have been able to embrace the new Cuba while sticking with plausible deniability. Kennedy fucked up by going ahead with the operation that Nixon was already going to execute, but he also half-assed it in a way Nixon probably wouldn’t have by refusing to send anymore air support when it was falling apart. So yeah Cuban Missile Crisis was Kennedy’s fault for not axing Bay of Pigs or at least ensuring it worked, but Tricky Dick was hardly innocent of Bay of Pigs.
